Mohegan

The Mohegan Tribe’s publications introduce spoken record-keeping, the history of Mohegan Church and the Tantaquidgeon Museum. These are community perspectives on preserving knowledge and sustaining institutions, with oral interpretations distinguished from written records and wider Indigenous traditions.

01

Identity and context

The Mohegan Tribe is a contemporary nation in Connecticut. Mohegan and Mohican are distinct identities.

Read the sources [1] The Mohegan Tribe

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Mohegan-authored histories, language reclamation and contemporary government. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] The Mohegan Tribe [2] mohegangaming.com [3] mohegan.nsn.us

03

Oral tradition as interpreted record-keeping

The Tribe describes oral traditions as records carried by trained culture-bearers and understood within a community able to respond to a telling. It also explains how interpretation can make older language intelligible to a later generation. This is the Tribe’s account of knowledge transmission, not a universal description of all Indigenous oral traditions; no private narrative is retold here.

Read the sources [1] The Mohegan Tribe

04

One building, several community roles

The Tribe traces Mohegan Church to an 1831 meeting house and describes later restoration and expansion. Its public account presents the building as a place for social, educational, political and religious functions. A modern photograph of the exterior illustrates this particular community institution; it does not imply that every Mohegan person follows one religion.

Read the sources [4] The Mohegan Tribe

05

Museum interpretation from a Mohegan perspective

The museum account recalls John, Harold and Gladys Tantaquidgeon’s work in founding the museum in 1931. It connects learning about Mohegan people with countering hostility and describes interpretation led by community members. The publication is an introduction to that work, rather than a fresh inspection of museum objects or every associated historical claim.

Read the sources [5] The Mohegan Tribe

Oral Traditions — the Tribe’s account of spoken record-keeping ↗

A short but substantive explanation presents oral traditions as community-held records interpreted by trained culture-bearers. It is the Tribe’s description of knowledge transmission, not a universal rule for every Indigenous tradition.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete introductory Oral Traditions prose, web-reader lines186–190. Linked Makiawisug and Moshup narratives, images, museum and videos not opened as part of this source review.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public prose read through the normal web reader. A separate automated public GET returned HTTP 403 and was not retried or bypassed. No private story, recording, interview or restricted cultural teaching inspected. Statements about community correction and interpreting older language are attributed to this publication; no oral narrative is retold or treated as a dated archaeological event.

The Mohegan Church — historical community institution ↗

The Tribe relates the 1831 meeting house and later restoration to community life. Religious, political, educational and social functions are described together without treating every Mohegan person as a member of one church.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete public main Church account, web-reader lines186–192; synthesis limited to founding, Lucy Teecomwas/Cynthia Hoscott’s land conveyance as attributed history, later renovation and institutional uses. Interior and ceremonial references read only as context, not reproduced.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public prose read through the normal web reader. A separate automated public GET returned HTTP 403 and was not retried or bypassed. No original deed, recognition petition, restoration file, interior, religious service or ceremonial object inspected. Continuous-title and legal conditions are not independently established. The modern exterior photograph is not evidence of universal religious affiliation or present property boundaries.

https://www.mohegan.nsn.us/about/our-tribal-history/historical-sites/the-mohegan-church

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Main museum historical and mission paragraphs, web-reader lines186–196; hours, admission, group appointments, surrounding structures and linked object pages excluded from synthesis.
